title: Inline Speed Skating Wheels Explained: Size, Durometer and Choosing Between JUNK and MPC
thumbnail_text: Your wheels matter more than your bearings

scenes.heading: Inline Speed Skating Wheels Explained
scenes.sub: Size, firmness, rotation, and how to choose
scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will know how to choose the right wheel size and firmness for the skating you actually do. You will also learn how to make a set last longer. Bearings get most of the attention at any track. Skaters compare ceramics and argue about oil. But your wheels are the only part of your setup that touches the ground. They are what turn your effort into forward motion. Yet most skaters pick them because they were the ones in stock. Let's fix that.

scenes.heading: What your wheels decide
bullets: How much grip you get in a corner
How much rolling resistance you fight
How the skate feels on rough tarmac
How many kilometres a set lasts
scenes.narration: Wheels are the single biggest performance variable on an inline speed skate. They decide how much grip you have in a corner. They decide how much rolling resistance you fight on the straight. They change how the skate feels over rough tarmac. And they decide how many kilometres you get before you need a new set. Get the wheels right, and everything else in your setup works better. Get them wrong, and even the best bearings will not save you. So let's start with the first decision, which is size.

scenes.heading: Bigger wheels meet bumps at a shallower angle
scenes.narration: Here is a 90 millimetre wheel on the left and a 110 millimetre wheel on the right. Both meet the same bump. The bigger wheel meets it at a shallower angle, so it rolls over rough surfaces more easily. A larger wheel also covers more ground with every turn. On a smooth track or a good road, a 110 carries speed well and holds it with less effort once you are up to pace. But look at the axle height. The bigger wheel sits higher off the ground. That raises your centre of gravity, and the skate feels less planted and less responsive.

scenes.heading: Big wheels and small wheels
bullets: 110mm: carries speed on smooth, open roads
Bigger wheels are heavier to accelerate
90mm and 100mm: faster off the mark
Smaller wheels sit lower and feel connected
scenes.narration: Big wheels have real costs. They are heavier, so they take more work to accelerate. They take more work to swing through each stride. And they need a frame built to take them. Smaller wheels, at 90 or 100 millimetres, accelerate faster and sit lower. They give you a more connected, more controllable feel. On a tight indoor track, with constant corners and constant acceleration, that matters a lot. Many skaters chase 110 because the top marathon skaters use it. Then they end up slower on a technical track than they would be on 100.

scenes.heading: Choose your size honestly
bullets: Long roads and marathons: 110mm
Tight tracks and many corners: 90 or 100mm
Rough real world tarmac: larger diameter
Always check your frame's maximum size
scenes.narration: So ask what you actually skate, not what you hope to skate one day. Long, smooth, open roads and marathon distances point to 110. Tight indoor tracks, technical banked circuits and lots of hard acceleration out of corners point to 100 or 90. Rough road surfaces tend to reward the larger wheel, simply because it survives the bumps better. And one rule is not negotiable. Your frame decides the ceiling. Check the maximum wheel size your frame is rated for before you buy anything. This catches people out all the time.

scenes.heading: Durometer: grip versus roll
bullets: Durometer measures urethane hardness
Softer wheels deform more and grip more
Firmer wheels roll further and last longer
Firmer wheels pass more vibration to your feet
scenes.narration: The second decision is firmness, called durometer. It measures how hard the urethane is, on the A scale. It controls the oldest trade off in skating, which is grip against roll. A softer wheel deforms more where it meets the ground. That deformation gives you grip. It also loses energy as heat. A firmer wheel deforms less. It rolls with less resistance and lasts longer. But it gives you less grip and sends more vibration into your feet. There is no single correct answer. There is only the right answer for your surface, your weight and your skating.

scenes.heading: Where XFirm and XXFirm sit
scenes.narration: Most race wheels come in two firmness options. In the JUNK range, XFirm is rated 84 to 86A, and XXFirm is rated 86 to 88A. This scale runs from softer on the left to harder on the right. You can see the two ranges overlap at 86A. That is why skaters describe the difference as a shade, not a step. XFirm holds a little more. XXFirm rolls a little further. And notice the line at the bottom. Heat softens urethane. So a hot afternoon shifts every wheel towards the soft end of this scale.

scenes.heading: When to pick each compound
bullets: XFirm: slick, dusty or cool surfaces
XFirm: lighter skaters, developing corners
XXFirm: grippy roads and hot days
XXFirm: powerful skaters wanting roll and life
scenes.narration: Choose XFirm when you want more grip. That means slick or dusty surfaces, or a cool track. It also suits lighter skaters, and anyone still developing their corner technique who wants the wheel to help them. Choose XXFirm when the surface already has good grip, or when it is hot. It suits heavier or more powerful skaters who can overwhelm a softer wheel. Temperature matters more than most people admit, especially in Indian conditions. A wheel that feels perfect on an early winter morning can feel greasy and vague on hot afternoon tarmac. Skaters who race across seasons often keep two sets.

scenes.heading: JUNK and MPC: it comes down to feel
bullets: Both brands make wheels skaters win on
Pigment free urethane, 90 to 110mm options
Soft inner ring inside a harder outer body
Sets of eight, sold without bearings
scenes.narration: Now the brands. Both JUNK and MPC make wheels that world class skaters win on. One is not simply faster than the other. The JUNK Voodoo leaves out pigment entirely, so the urethane is exactly what the chemist intended, and it comes in 90, 100 and 110. The MPC Black Magic uses a softer inner ring inside a harder outer layer, so it flexes for grip while the outer body keeps rolling. The real difference is feel, and feel is personal. If you can try a friend's set first, do it. Remember that sets come as eight wheels without bearings, so plan for sixteen bearings and spacers.

scenes.heading: Rotate and flip: free speed
bullets: Inside edges wear faster than outside edges
Swap positions and flip the worn side out
Every couple of weeks if you train often
Check urethane, hubs and bearings as you go
scenes.narration: Wheels never wear evenly. Your inside edges take more punishment, because that is where you push. Left alone, a wheel cones, with a sharp inside edge and a flat outside. That gives you unpredictable grip in corners and wastes urethane you paid for. So swap each wheel to a new position and flip it, so the worn side faces out. The exact pattern matters less than doing it regularly. Every couple of weeks is a good start if you train several times a week. If you can feel a sharp lip with your thumb, you waited too long. While the wheels are off, check for chunking, cracked hubs and gritty bearings.

scenes.heading: Match the wheel to the skating you actually do
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: To make a set last, keep it clean, store it somewhere cool and out of the sun, and match the compound to your surface. Here is the short version. Pick your size for the surface and the skating you actually do. Pick your firmness for your surface, your weight and the temperature. Rotate on a schedule, and keep your bearings clean while you are in there. The full wheel guide, with answers to common questions, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
